record.program_name: HACSJ public housing repositioning and co-development (Delta Community Developers Corp.)
record.administering_agency: Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin and Delta Community Developers Corp. (DCDC), its nonprofit instrumentality
record.typical_award_size: HACSJ is repositioning its 910-unit public housing portfolio through RAD, Section 18 and mixed-finance deals and is itself the county's most active supportive housing developer. Pipeline from the FY 2026-27 Annual Plan and development page: Tracy Apartments Phases I and II (55 units each, replacing 17 demolished Tracy Homes units; sources include Health Plan of San Joaquin, HOME, Capital Fund loan, Freddie Mac permanent loan, U.S. Bank, LIHTC); Lodi Commons and Danny Drive (110 senior units each in two phases); Edison House (33 PSH units, Homekey+, Stockton PIP, HHAP); Grant Street Apartments (24 behavioral health units, MHSA, HHAP, ARPA); Sierra Vista Phase III (106 units, Section 18 disposition of 26 units in process, up to 80 approved vacancies); Conway Homes phased redevelopment. Sierra Vista Phase I was co-developed with CCHC, and HACSJ has sought a development partner for Sonora Square.
record.affordability_requirement: Public housing and PBV income limits with long-term use restrictions under RAD or Section 18 conversion; LIHTC restrictions on mixed-finance phases.
record.next_deadline: Partner solicitations are issued project by project on hacsj.org procurement; none open as of November 7, 2026.
record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). For outside developers HACSJ matters in three ways: as a PBV source, as a co-developer or ground lessor on repositioned public housing sites in Stockton, Tracy and Lodi, and as a competitor for the same County HOME, HHAP, Health Net and Regional Housing Fund dollars (Lodi Commons took $3 million of the $11.85 million Round 1 fund). Davis-Bacon and state prevailing wage apply to mixed-finance public housing work. HACSJ also operates farm labor housing in Lodi, French Camp and Thornton. Source is the HACSJ development page, supplemented by the 2026-27 Annual Plan and the 2025-2029 5-Year Plan (hacsj.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/05/10.1.25-5-Year-Plan.pdf).
eligible_project_detail: public housing redevelopment (RAD, Section 18, mixed finance)
co-development with private or nonprofit partners

record.program_name: Behavioral Health Services Act (BHSA) Integrated Plan FY 2026-29, housing interventions
record.administering_agency: San Joaquin County Behavioral Health Services (Health Care Services Agency)
record.typical_award_size: Three-year plan totaling $295,750,706 approved June 2, 2026 (5-0). The County requested a transfer of 7% from the housing component to Behavioral Health Services and Supports, leaving housing interventions at 23% of BHSA funds. Estimated housing intervention expenditures: $18,790,266 in year one and $42,013,536 in year two; the continuum table shows housing services of $37.0 million, $41.6 million and $37.8 million across the three years. Planned uses: project-based rental subsidies for about 150 people a year (64 permanent, 86 interim; 350 units), operating subsidies for about 116 people (228 units, property management staffing for SRO and transitional-to-permanent apartments), landlord outreach and mitigation for about 100, and two capital projects (a 50-unit tiny home project and the 33-unit Edison House, both braided with other funds, unit availability June 30, 2027, BHSA share capped at $450,000 per unit).
record.per_unit_cap: BHSA capital share capped at $450,000 per unit by DHCS policy; counties may spend up to 25% of housing interventions on capital.
record.affordability_requirement: Individuals with serious behavioral health conditions who are homeless or at risk; at least 50% of housing intervention funds for chronically homeless households; PSH setting types and Housing First.
record.next_deadline: Plan effective July 1, 2026 through June 30, 2029 with annual updates each June. Behavioral Health Services completed a request for qualifications for housing developers in 2025-26 (RFQ 25107) and will work with the pre-qualified pool: Central Valley Low Income Housing Corporation, Delta Community Developers Corporation, Domus Development LLC, Mahogany and Oak Real Estate, Mutual Housing California, RHCB Development LP, Self-Help Enterprises and Visionary Home Builders of California.
record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). BHSA is the County's largest discretionary housing stream and the realistic source of project-based operating subsidy for PSH units in the unincorporated county and Stockton; capital is limited to the two named projects, so new deals should pitch rental or operating subsidies for behavioral health set-aside units rather than construction money. Behavioral Health Services also carries Homekey+ (Bridge to Home, $15,900,896 agreement with CVLIHC approved January 13, 2026) and Behavioral Health Bridge Housing Round 3 contracts, and is building the SJ BeWell campus with a $38.2 million BHCIP Round 2 award (March 2026). Pre-qualification through the BHS RFQ is the entry point for developers. The Board file (source) links the board order, the 490-page DHCS Integrated Plan submission (FileOpen.aspx?Type=4&ID=45761) and the June 2, 2026 presentation.
eligible_project_detail: operating subsidies for interim and permanent settings

record.program_name: Development impact fee deferral for affordable housing (Housing Element program, unincorporated county)
record.administering_agency: San Joaquin County Community Development Department and Public Works
record.typical_award_size: Typical planning and development impact fees for a multifamily unit in the unincorporated county were about $20,000 to $20,500 per unit in 2023 (County fees of roughly $9,200 to $9,650 plus County facilities $1,564, regional transportation $2,664, habitat mitigation $1,929, school $4,041 and fire $620). The 2023-2031 Housing Element commits the County to process fee deferrals for projects affordable to lower-income households and to study fee waivers or reductions for affordable projects; no fee waiver fund or standing deferral ordinance was found.
record.affordability_requirement: Projects affordable to lower-income households as defined in the Housing Element programs; terms set case by case.
record.next_deadline: Request with the entitlement application; the Housing Element says the County will implement a deferral or reduction policy within three months of finding it feasible.
record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Impact fees in the unincorporated county are low compared with Bay Area counties, so deferral is worth less than $20,000 per unit of carry; the larger cost issue is extending water and sewer to sites. Habitat mitigation (SJMSCP) and regional transportation fees are set by other agencies and are not waived by the County. Marked needs_confirmation because the Housing Element (opened) describes the policy as a commitment to study and implement, and no adopted deferral ordinance or fee schedule page was opened this pass; confirm with Community Development.

record.program_name: County-owned and surplus land for affordable housing
record.administering_agency: San Joaquin County General Services (real property), with Behavioral Health Services and Veterans Services for sponsored projects
record.typical_award_size: No standing County land program. Known actions: a Surplus Land Act notice of availability for about four acres of County-owned land adjacent to Gianone Park in Stockton for deed-restricted affordable housing by sale or long-term ground lease (posted November 20, 2025, offers due January 30, 2026, Board approval required); Victory Gardens, 49 veteran PSH units built on 2.5 acres of County land in French Camp; a proposed campus-style veterans housing village in French Camp near San Joaquin General Hospital pursued with a Homekey+ application in 2026.
record.affordability_requirement: Surplus Land Act priority for affordable housing developers with at least 25% of units at or below 80% AMI (Government Code 54222.5) or deeper restrictions negotiated with the County.
record.next_deadline: Gianone Park offering closed January 30, 2026; outcome not posted. Watch the County Purchasing bid page (sjgov.org/department/pss/bids, Public Purchase) and HCD's surplus land notices map for future notices.
record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). County land has been the basis for the county's veteran PSH projects and is the most likely form of County contribution to a new deal because the County has no capital fund. Marked needs_confirmation because the Gianone Park notice was read on a third-party procurement aggregator (source) and the County's own bid posting (sjgov.org/gems bidView bidId=206984) returned 404 on November 7, 2026; confirm with County General Services.

record.program_name: HOME-ARP allocation, San Joaquin Urban County
record.administering_agency: San Joaquin County Human Services Agency, Neighborhood Preservation Division
record.typical_award_size: HOME-ARP is being committed to rental development: $2,000,000 of County HOME-ARP is in the Lodi Commons capital stack (55 senior units, HACSJ, release of funds requested November 20, 2026). The County HOME-ARP Allocation Plan is posted on the Annual Plan page; total allocation not restated in documents opened this pass.

record.next_deadline: One-time ARPA allocation; expenditure deadline September 30, 2030. Remaining balance, if any, would be offered through the annual CDBG, HOME and ESG NOFA.
record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). HOME-ARP is a one-time source and the County has already placed $2 million of it in Lodi Commons alongside three years of regular HOME, HHAP, Health Net and Regional Housing Fund money. Davis-Bacon applies at 12 or more HOME-assisted units. Source is the County's Lodi Commons FONSI and request for release of funds (November 4, 2026); the HOME-ARP plan itself (sjchsa.org Portals HOME-ARP-Plan-.pdf) was not opened, hence needs_confirmation on the total allocation.

record.program_name: Health Net and Health Plan of San Joaquin housing investments (Medi-Cal plan capital grants)
record.administering_agency: Health Net (Centene) and Health Plan of San Joaquin, in partnership with HACSJ and the San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund
record.typical_award_size: Health Net granted $3,000,000 to the San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund (2026, $2,850,000 net available for loans) and $2,000,000 directly to Lodi Commons; Health Plan of San Joaquin is listed as a source for Tracy Apartments Phase I. Awards have been $2 million to $3 million per commitment.
record.affordability_requirement: Low-income and Medi-Cal member households; Health Net funds in the regional fund are flexible but prioritize low-income units.
record.next_deadline: No public application; commitments negotiated with the plans and routed through the Regional Housing Fund or directly to HACSJ projects.
record.layering_notes: San Joaquin County has no county housing trust fund, no county housing bond and no inclusionary ordinance; the County's own capital for multifamily is limited to HUD pass-through funds administered by the Human Services Agency Neighborhood Preservation Division (sjchsa.org), while the regional gap lender is the SJCOG-sponsored San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund and the main voucher and development partner is the Housing Authority of the County of San Joaquin (HACSJ). Managed care plan money is the newest soft source in the county and has shown up in every 2026 capital stack (Lodi Commons, Tracy Apartments, the Regional Housing Fund). It is grant money and does not by itself trigger prevailing wage, but it is always paired with public funds that do. Recorded at county level because the plans are county Medi-Cal plans and the money flows through countywide vehicles; figures are from the SJCOG March 11, 2026 announcement (source), the June 18, 2026 fund packet and the Lodi Commons FONSI.

record.program_name: CDBG entitlement, City of Lodi (2026-27 Annual Action Plan and annual CDBG application cycle)
record.administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department, Neighborhood Services Division (CDBG administration consultant Michael Baker International)
record.typical_award_size: 2026-27 CDBG award $665,263 (2025-26 $655,037; 2024-25 $675,615): capital projects $434,263 including Public Works $235,000, DCDC/HACSJ Salas Park (Lodi Commons) $115,000 and $84,263 unassigned; CBO services $98,000 (15% cap); admin $133,000 including fair housing. 2026-27 cycle anticipated about $310,000 for capital and infrastructure applications. record.per_unit_cap: None; HOME limits do not apply because Lodi has no HOME allocation.
record.affordability_requirement: HUD CDBG national objective (low and moderate income benefit); Consolidated Plan 2024-2028 goal to preserve and increase affordable housing through rehabilitation, land acquisition or partnerships with housing developers.
record.next_deadline: 2026-27 applications ran December 8, 2025 to January 27, 2026; the 2027-28 cycle should open about December 2026 with applications due late January 2027 and funds available July 1, 2027. 2025-26 CAPER hearing was September 2, 2026. Contact NeighborhoodServices@lodi.gov.
record.layering_notes: Lodi is a CDBG entitlement city but not a HOME participating jurisdiction; HOME for Lodi projects comes from the San Joaquin Urban County NOFA (Lodi Commons received $230,024 plus $500,000 program income in 2026-27 and $2 million HOME-ARP, county records). City CDBG contributions to housing are small infrastructure or predevelopment pieces ($115,000 to Salas Park in 2026-27), so treat CDBG as a sub-$250,000 layer. Lodi joined the SJCOG San Joaquin Regional Housing Fund by resolution on July 17, 2024 and gets HHAP Round 4 ($652,126) and Round 5 subrecipient funds for shelter and transitional housing. Read from the City CDBG page and the 2026-27 Annual Action Plan PDF.
eligible_project_detail: site acquisition and infrastructure for affordable housing

record.program_name: Lodi Housing Element 2023-2031 incentive programs (Program 1.6 fee waivers, reductions or deferrals for infill at 20 or more units per acre; Program 1.12 incentives for special needs housing; Program 1.5 funding applications)
record.administering_agency: City of Lodi Community Development Department
record.typical_award_size: Not yet adopted as a standing program. Program 1.6 commits the City to adopt by 2025 one or more incentives for infill housing at 20 or more units per acre: parking credits, fee waivers, reductions or deferrals when financially feasible, priority processing. Program 1.12 commits to incentives (reduced standards, fee waivers or financial assistance) for housing for persons with disabilities by 2026. Program 1.5 sets a goal of the City securing $1 million in state or federal housing funds by 2028 and $2 million by 2031. Housing Element impact fee estimate: about $18,948 development impact fees plus $11,468 building fees per single-family home; multifamily fees lower per unit.
record.affordability_requirement: Program 1.6 objective: incentivize 100 extremely low, 200 very low and 200 low income units on infill parcels; Program 1.12 objective 40 special needs units.
record.next_deadline: No adopting resolution found through 2026-11-08; the Housing Element deadline for Program 1.6 (2025) has passed, so ask Planning (209) 333-6711 whether a fee deferral or waiver policy is before Council. Lodi is also adding Chapter 15.69 (Agricultural Mitigation Fee) and 15.70 (Parkland Dedication and In-Lieu) in October 2026, which add costs rather than relief.
record.layering_notes: Lodi has no housing trust fund, inclusionary ordinance, in-lieu fee or housing successor fund; HOME comes only through the County. Until Program 1.6 is adopted, the only fee relief is state law (ADU fee exemptions, SB 937 fee timing). Expect County HOME plus SJRHF, HACSJ PBVs and BHSA (county records) to carry gap financing, with City CDBG for off-site infrastructure. Programs read from the adopted 2023-2031 Housing Element PDF on lodi.gov (HCD certified April 11, 2024).
eligible_project_detail: new construction (infill, 20 or more units per acre)
